feedback: If the learner predicts the thousandth is bigger 'because 1000 beats 100', do not just correct — have them physically lay one thousandth against one hundredth so the size difference is visible, then restate the rule 'more parts means each is smaller'.
For 0.05 vs 0.005, if they pick 0.005, point to the split: 0.005 is 5 thousandths while 0.05 is 50 thousandths (ten times larger); have them count how many thousandths are in each.
Confirm success when the learner states that a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth and can explain why the larger number 1000 does not make the part larger.
activities.intendedInsight: More, smaller parts means each part is smaller: a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100, overturning 'bigger denominator, bigger part'.
learnerActions: Before comparing, predict which is bigger, one hundredth or one thousandth, and say WHY in words.
Take one hundredth and split it into ten equal parts; identify each part as one thousandth.
Lay a single thousandth beside a whole hundredth and describe what you see — the thousandth is tiny next to the hundredth.
Reconcile this with your prediction: even though 1000 is a bigger number than 100, a thousandth is a smaller amount because it comes from cutting into more, smaller parts.
Compare 0.05 and 0.005 directly and state which is bigger and why, when both use the digit 5.
activities.title: Split a hundredth and compare sizes to break whole-number bias

feedback: If the learner writes 0.25 for 25 thousandths, return to the chart: thousandths is the third place after the point, so 25 must occupy hundredths and thousandths, leaving tenths empty and needing a 0.
If they write 0.0025, check column by column: the 5 should sit in thousandths (third place), not further right.
Confirm success when they both write 0.025 correctly and explain, using the chart, why the zero after the point is needed and why 25/100 and 25/1000 differ.
activities.intendedInsight: The place a value occupies, not just the digits, fixes the written decimal; the placeholder zero in 0.025 holds the empty tenths position so the 2 lands in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths.
learnerActions: Using a place-value chart with columns ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths, write 25 thousandths: place the 2 in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths.
Fill the empty tenths column with a 0 and write the decimal 0.025, then explain that the zero holds the empty tenths place.
Contrast the set 25/10 = 2.5, 25/100 = 0.25, 25/1000 = 0.025, and describe how the place of the value decides where the digits land and how many leading places are filled.
Write a second example, e.g. 35 thousandths = 35/1000 = 0.035, and say why there is one placeholder zero straight after the decimal point (in the tenths place).
activities.title: Write thousandths and justify the placeholder zero

feedback: If the learner says 10 thousandths = 1 tenth, build it in stages: 'How many thousandths in a hundredth? And how many hundredths in a tenth? So how many thousandths in a tenth?'
Have them count on a subdivided line through both levels to see the two steps accumulate to 100.
Confirm success when they answer 100 thousandths per tenth and can name both tenfold steps that compose it.
activities.intendedInsight: Getting from thousandths to tenths is two tenfold steps, not one: 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth and 100 thousandths = 1 tenth; the nesting composes rather than applying a single ×10.
learnerActions: State and show that 10 thousandths make 1 hundredth (one ÷10 subdivision).
Then show that 10 hundredths make 1 tenth, so composing the two steps gives 100 thousandths = 1 tenth.
Continue the chain to 1000 thousandths = 1 whole, naming each tenfold step.
Answer the trap question 'How many thousandths are in one tenth?' and justify 100 (two tenfold steps), explaining why 10 is wrong (it skips a step).
activities.title: Compose two tenfold steps: 10 and 100 thousandths

feedback: For the comparison item, if the learner selects 0.005 citing 1000 > 100, route back to the split-and-compare activity to re-establish 'more parts, smaller each'.
For 25/1000, if they omit the placeholder zero, return to the place-value chart activity.
Treat the 'why' answers as diagnostic: a learner who answers correctly but cannot explain the two-step nesting or the placeholder still needs the composing and notation activities.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct answers plus a stated reason distinguish genuine grasp of the recursive tenth-of-a-tenth-of-a-tenth structure from a memorised conversion or digit-copying.
learnerActions: Complete 25/1000 = 0.0__ and justify where the 2 and 5 sit and why the zero is there.
Complete '100 thousandths = __ tenth' and explain the two-step reasoning.
Decide which is bigger, 0.05 or 0.005, and give a reason that does not rely on 'more digits means bigger'.
Place 0.345 between 0.34 and 0.35 by stating how many equal steps are in the gap and which step 0.345 is.
activities.title: Check and diagnose with targeted questions
